# Reconciliation and Cross-verification {#sec-recon}

A district health society keeps its money in one bank account. Its cashier writes every cheque, every e-payment and every receipt into the cash book. The bank keeps its own record of the same account, and sends it as a statement. The two records describe the same money, so at the end of the year they should agree. They seldom do. A cheque written on 28 March reaches the bank in April. The bank deducts its charges without telling anyone. A clerk types ₹54,320 where the cheque says ₹45,320. And once in a while, money leaves the account on a cheque that the cash book has never heard of.

Matching two such records is called **reconciliation**. It looks simple. Earlier we learnt to join two tables on a common key (@sec-joins). But a cash book and a bank statement have no common key. The cash book writes "CHQ 004512" and the bank writes "4512". The amounts differ by a rupee because one side rounded. The dates differ by a few days because cheques take time to clear. One credit in the bank settles three bills that the cashier entered separately. An exact join handles only the tidy part of the problem.

The same task appears all over Indian audit, under the wider name of **cross-verification**. We check one record against an independent record that should agree with it. The input tax credit claimed by a business is checked against what its suppliers reported. A department's expenditure is checked against the treasury's figures. A scheme's list of payments is checked against the bank's list of credits. When two independent sources agree, we gain real assurance. When they disagree, the difference is often where the problem lies.

In this chapter we first learn the ideas behind a reconciliation. We then match a cash book with a bank statement in five steps, each step removing what it has matched. We study what is left, age it and value it, and present the familiar bank reconciliation statement. A second use case checks input tax credit against the suppliers' returns, and a short third example compares a department's figures with the treasury's. @sec-jet, the previous chapter, checked that a ledger is complete before testing it. The same checks apply here, and we do not repeat them.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}


## The idea of reconciliation {#sec-recon-idea}

When we put two records of the same money side by side, every item falls into one of three groups.

- **Matched items.** The item is in both records, with the same amount. A cheque of ₹25,000 written on 3 June and paid by the bank on 5 June is matched.
- **Timing differences.** The item is in one record and will reach the other soon, without anyone doing anything. A cheque written on 30 March and paid by the bank on 4 April is an **unpresented cheque** at 31 March. Money deposited on 31 March and credited on 2 April is a **deposit in transit**. Timing differences clear by themselves.
- **Permanent differences.** The item is in one record and will never reach the other unless someone acts. Bank charges that the office has not entered in its cash book stay missing until the office enters them. So do typing errors, cheques that were cancelled but never reversed, and irregular items such as an unauthorised withdrawal.

Every difference must be explained, and no item should stay in the reconciliation for long. An unpresented cheque of last week is normal. An unpresented cheque of last July is not. Banks do not pay a cheque presented more than three months after its date, so such a cheque is **stale**. It should be cancelled and the amount written back in the cash book. Very old reconciling items are a classic hiding place. A cheque that was never meant to be paid, or a receipt that never reached the bank, can sit in the reconciliation for years, explained each month as "timing". So we always **age** the reconciling items, and look hardest at the old ones.

The table below sums up the plan of the chapter.

| Step | What it matches | Technique |
|------------------|---------------------------------|--------------------------|
| 1 | Same cheque number and same amount | Equality join on a cleaned reference |
| 2 | Amount within ₹1, date within a few days | Inequality join with `between()` |
| 3 | One item for each item, when several could match | Sorting candidates and picking greedily |
| 4 | One bank credit for several receipts | Searching small combinations with `combn()` |
| 5 | Cheque numbers typed wrongly | String distance with `stringdist()` |
| Left | Items in only one record | `anti_join()`, classified, aged and valued |

: The steps of matching a cash book with a bank statement {#tbl-recon-steps}

## Our data, a cash book and a bank statement {#sec-recon-data}

Our auditee is the District Health Society of an imaginary district, Keshavnagar. It receives grants from the State Health Society every quarter, collects fees and rents, and pays suppliers, contractors and staff. All of this passes through one savings bank account. We have received three things for 2024-25.

- `cash_book` is the bank column of the society's cash book. Each row has an id `cb_id`, the `date`, the `particulars`, a reference `ref`, and the amount as a `receipt` or a `payment`. Cheques are written "CHQ 004512". E-payments carry the society's own advice number, such as "EP/24-25/0001", and receipts the receipt number.
- `bank` is the bank statement for the same year, with an id `bs_id`, the `date`, the bank's `narration`, the cheque number `ref` for cheques, the `withdrawal` or `deposit`, and the running `balance`.
- `bank_apr` is the bank statement for April 2025, the month after the year end.

The reconciliation at 31 March 2024 had no outstanding items, so the cash book and the bank both opened the year with the same balance, `opening`. Most transactions are routine. Cheques take one to five days to clear, and some take longer. E-payments are debited the same day or within two days. Cheques deposited take one to three days to be credited. Twelve shops in the hospital complex each pay the same rent of ₹15,000 every month. These are the planted cases.

1. **Unpresented cheques.** Cheques written in the last week of March reach the bank in April.
2. **Deposits in transit.** Cheques deposited on the last days of March are credited in April.
3. **Bank charges and interest not booked.** The society entered the bank's charges and interest until December. It did not enter those of January to March.
4. **A transposition error.** A cheque of ₹45,320 is entered in the cash book as ₹54,320.
5. **A cheque that never reached the bank.** A large cheque to a contractor in November 2024 was never presented.
6. **A stale cheque.** A small cheque of July 2024 is still unpresented at the year end.
7. **A debit in the bank that is not in the cash book.** Cash was withdrawn on a "self" cheque from the society's own cheque book. The cash book has no entry for it.
8. **One credit for several receipts.** One party paid three bills by a single transfer, and the cashier entered three receipts. Another party paid two bills at once.
9. **Cheque numbers written differently.** The cash book writes "CHQ 004512", the bank "4512". Four cheque numbers were also typed wrongly in the cash book.

There is also genuine noise. E-payments are rounded to the rupee, while the cash book sometimes shows paise. Dates differ by a few days in normal clearing.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the cash book and the bank statements"
set.seed(2503)
fy_days <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-31"), by = "day")
open_days <- fy_days[wday(fy_days, week_start = 1) <= 6]       # banks open Monday to Saturday
next_open <- function(d) d + if_else(wday(d, week_start = 1) == 7, 1, 0)

vendors <- c("Shree Ganesh Traders", "Om Sai Suppliers", "Gupta Stationery Mart", "Kaveri Medical Agencies",
             "Narmada Diagnostics", "Prakash Electricals", "Sunrise Printers", "Jai Durga Transport",
             "Anand Computers", "Vinayak Furniture House", "Balaji Caterers", "Shakti Security Services",
             "Mehta Pharma Distributors", "Rana Builders", "Patel Oxygen Suppliers",
             "Nirmal Cleaning Services", "Lakshmi Tent House", "Sharma Auto Works", "Deep Lab Instruments")
parties <- c("Shiva Medical Stores", "Mahalaxmi Caterers", "Arogya Path Labs", "City Care Pharmacy",
             "Green Leaf Canteen", "Sanjeevani Chemists", "Krishna Blood Bank", "Vardaan Opticals",
             "Sapna Xerox Centre", "Ujala Diagnostic Centre", "Ramesh Ambulance Service", "Neel Kamal Dairy")

# 1. Cheque payments, numbered in series, cleared in one to five days, some later
n_chq <- 961
chq <- tibble(date = sort(sample(open_days, n_chq, TRUE)), no = 4101:(4100 + n_chq),
              amount = round(rlnorm(n_chq, log(38000), 0.9)), party = sample(vendors, n_chq, TRUE),
              lag = sample(1:5, n_chq, TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.3, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1)), case = NA_character_)
late <- sample(n_chq, 30); chq$lag[late] <- sample(6:12, 30, TRUE)
ye <- chq$date >= as.Date("2025-03-25"); chq$lag[ye] <- sample(3:9, sum(ye), TRUE)

# Planted 7. A self cheque, left out of the cash book
i_unauth <- which.min(abs(chq$date - as.Date("2025-01-17")))
chq$amount[i_unauth] <- 250000; chq$party[i_unauth] <- "Self"; chq$case[i_unauth] <- "Unauthorised"
# Planted 4. A transposition error
i_trans <- which.min(abs(chq$date - as.Date("2024-09-12")))
chq$amount[i_trans] <- 45320; chq$case[i_trans] <- "Transposition"; chq$lag[i_trans] <- 3
# Planted 5. A large cheque never presented
i_never <- which.min(abs(chq$date - as.Date("2024-11-23")))
chq$amount[i_never] <- 485000; chq$party[i_never] <- "Rana Builders"; chq$case[i_never] <- "Never presented"
# Planted 6. A stale cheque
i_stale <- which.min(abs(chq$date - as.Date("2024-07-12")))
chq$amount[i_stale] <- 18600; chq$party[i_stale] <- "Gupta Stationery Mart"; chq$case[i_stale] <- "Stale"
# Planted 9. Four cheque numbers typed wrongly, on cheques presented late
cand_typo <- setdiff(which(chq$date < as.Date("2025-02-15")), c(i_unauth, i_trans, i_never, i_stale))
i_typo <- sample(cand_typo, 4)
chq$case[i_typo] <- "Typo"; chq$lag[i_typo] <- c(11, 15, 9, 19)

swap_two <- function(s) { ch <- strsplit(s, "")[[1]]; ch[2:3] <- ch[3:2]; paste(ch, collapse = "") }
chq <- chq |>
  mutate(cb_no = as.character(no), bank_date = next_open(date + lag), bank_amount = amount)
chq$cb_no[i_typo] <- c(swap_two(chq$cb_no[i_typo[1]]), as.character(chq$no[i_typo[2]] + 1000),
                       swap_two(chq$cb_no[i_typo[3]]), sub(".$", "8", chq$cb_no[i_typo[4]]))
chq$amount[i_trans] <- 54320                       # the cash book side of the transposition
chq$bank_date[c(i_never, i_stale)] <- NA
chq$bank_date[i_unauth] <- next_open(chq$date[i_unauth] + 1)

# 2. E-payments, debited in up to two days. The bank pays in whole rupees.
n_ep <- 1100
ep <- tibble(date = sort(sample(open_days, n_ep, TRUE)), amount = round(rlnorm(n_ep, log(52000), 1), 2),
             party = sample(c(vendors, "Contractual staff salary", "ASHA honorarium"), n_ep, TRUE),
             lag = sample(0:2, n_ep, TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.35, 0.15)))
whole <- runif(n_ep) < 0.92
ep$amount[whole] <- round(ep$amount[whole])
ep <- ep |>
  mutate(no = row_number(), bank_amount = round(amount), bank_date = next_open(date + lag),
         utr = paste0("N", sample(10^8:(10^9 - 1), n_ep)))

# 3. Receipts by transfer or by cheque, monthly shop rents, and quarterly grants
n_rc <- 700
rc <- tibble(date = sort(sample(open_days, n_rc, TRUE)), party = sample(parties, n_rc, TRUE),
             amount = round(rlnorm(n_rc, log(30000), 0.9)),
             mode = sample(c("NEFT", "CLG"), n_rc, TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)), case = NA_character_)
rent <- expand_grid(m = seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-01"), by = "month"),
                    party = sprintf("Shop no %02d, hospital complex", 1:12)) |>
  mutate(date = next_open(m + sample(0:6, n(), TRUE)), amount = 15000, mode = "NEFT",
         case = NA_character_) |>
  select(-m)
grants <- tibble(date = as.Date(c("2024-04-10", "2024-07-08", "2024-10-07", "2025-01-09")),
                 party = "State Health Society", amount = c(36000000, 34500000, 35800000, 37200000),
                 mode = "RTGS", case = NA_character_)
# Planted 8. One transfer for three bills, and one for two
m3 <- tibble(date = as.Date("2024-12-11"), party = "Shiva Medical Stores", amount = c(42350, 18920, 27600),
             mode = "NEFT", case = "Three receipts, one credit")
m2 <- tibble(date = as.Date("2024-08-21"), party = "Mahalaxmi Caterers", amount = c(31500, 26750),
             mode = "NEFT", case = "Two receipts, one credit")
# Planted 2. Cheques deposited at the year end
dit <- tibble(date = as.Date(c("2025-03-29", "2025-03-31", "2025-03-31")),
              party = c("Arogya Path Labs", "Ujala Diagnostic Centre", "City Care Pharmacy"),
              amount = c(64800, 112500, 38250), mode = "CLG", case = NA_character_)
rc <- bind_rows(rc, rent, grants, m3, m2, dit) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(no = row_number(), lag = if_else(mode == "CLG", sample(1:3, n(), TRUE), 0L),
         bank_date = next_open(date + lag),
         utr = paste0(if_else(mode == "RTGS", "R", "N"), sample(10^8:(10^9 - 1), n())))

# 4. Bank charges and interest. Planted 3. Those after December are not in the cash book.
months <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-01"), by = "month")
chg <- bind_rows(
  tibble(bank_date = ceiling_date(months, "month") - 1, amount = 590, narr = "SERVICE CHGS INCL GST"),
  tibble(bank_date = as.Date(c("2024-06-30", "2024-09-30", "2024-12-31", "2025-03-31")), amount = 17.7,
         narr = "SMS ALERT CHGS QTR"),
  tibble(bank_date = as.Date(c("2024-05-14", "2024-10-03", "2025-02-20")), amount = 236,
         narr = "CHQ BOOK ISSUE CHGS")) |>
  mutate(booked = bank_date <= as.Date("2024-12-31"))
int <- tibble(bank_date = as.Date(c("2024-09-30", "2025-03-31")), amount = c(212436, 238914),
              booked = c(TRUE, FALSE))

opening <- 12000000

# ---- The cash book ----
cash_book <- bind_rows(
  chq |> filter(is.na(case) | case != "Unauthorised") |>
    transmute(date, particulars = paste("Paid to", party), ref = paste0("CHQ ", str_pad(cb_no, 6, pad = "0")),
              receipt = 0, payment = amount),
  ep |> transmute(date, particulars = paste("Paid to", party), ref = sprintf("EP/24-25/%04d", no),
                  receipt = 0, payment = amount),
  rc |> transmute(date, particulars = paste("Received from", party), ref = sprintf("RCPT/%04d", no),
                  receipt = amount, payment = 0),
  chg |> filter(booked) |> transmute(date = bank_date, particulars = "Bank charges as per statement",
                                     ref = NA_character_, receipt = 0, payment = amount),
  int |> filter(booked) |> transmute(date = bank_date, particulars = "Interest credited by bank",
                                     ref = NA_character_, receipt = amount, payment = 0)) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(cb_id = sprintf("CB%04d", row_number()), .before = 1)

# ---- The bank's record, for 2024-25 and April 2025 ----
bank_all <- bind_rows(
  chq |> filter(!is.na(bank_date)) |>
    transmute(date = bank_date,
              narration = if_else(party == "Self", paste("CASH WDL SELF CHQ", no),
                                  paste("CHQ PAID", no, str_to_upper(party))),
              ref = as.character(no), withdrawal = bank_amount, deposit = 0),
  ep |> transmute(date = bank_date, narration = paste("NEFT DR", utr, str_to_upper(party)),
                  ref = NA_character_, withdrawal = bank_amount, deposit = 0),
  rc |> filter(is.na(case)) |>
    transmute(date = bank_date, narration = paste(mode, "CR", utr, str_to_upper(party)),
              ref = NA_character_, withdrawal = 0, deposit = amount),
  rc |> filter(!is.na(case)) |>
    summarise(date = max(bank_date), narration = paste("NEFT CR", first(utr), str_to_upper(first(party))),
              withdrawal = 0, deposit = sum(amount), .by = case) |>
    select(-case),
  chg |> transmute(date = bank_date, narration = narr, ref = NA_character_, withdrawal = amount, deposit = 0),
  int |> transmute(date = bank_date, narration = "INT CR SB ACCOUNT", ref = NA_character_,
                   withdrawal = 0, deposit = amount)) |>
  arrange(date)

# April 2025 also has the society's own April transactions
apr_days <- open_days[1:22] + 365
apr_new <- tibble(date = sort(sample(apr_days, 45, TRUE)), kind = sample(c("CHQ", "NEFT DR", "NEFT CR"), 45, TRUE),
                  amount = round(rlnorm(45, log(40000), 0.9))) |>
  mutate(no = if_else(kind == "CHQ", 5062L + cumsum(kind == "CHQ"), NA_integer_),
         party = if_else(kind == "NEFT CR", sample(parties, 45, TRUE), sample(vendors, 45, TRUE)),
         narration = if_else(kind == "CHQ", paste("CHQ PAID", no, str_to_upper(party)),
                             paste(kind, paste0("N", sample(10^8:(10^9 - 1), 45)), str_to_upper(party))),
         ref = if_else(kind == "CHQ", as.character(no), NA_character_),
         withdrawal = if_else(kind == "NEFT CR", 0, amount), deposit = if_else(kind == "NEFT CR", amount, 0)) |>
  select(date, narration, ref, withdrawal, deposit)

bank <- bank_all |>
  filter(date <= as.Date("2025-03-31")) |>
  mutate(bs_id = sprintf("BS%04d", row_number()), .before = 1,
         balance = opening + cumsum(deposit - withdrawal))
bank_apr <- bank_all |>
  filter(date > as.Date("2025-03-31")) |>
  bind_rows(apr_new) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(balance = last(bank$balance) + cumsum(deposit - withdrawal))

rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("cash_book", "bank", "bank_apr", "opening")))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
lakh <- function(x) round(x / 1e5, 1)
crore <- function(x) round(x / 1e7, 2)
inr <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  s <- formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = digits)
  int <- sub("\\..*$", "", s)
  dec <- if (digits > 0) sub("^[^.]*", "", s) else ""
  grp <- vapply(int, function(v) {
    n <- nchar(v)
    if (n <= 3) return(v)
    head <- gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(v, 1, n - 3), perl = TRUE)
    paste0(head, ",", substr(v, n - 2, n))
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
  paste0(grp, dec)
}
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
fdate <- function(d) paste(day(d), format(d, "%B %Y"))
```

Let us look at the two records.

```{r}
cash_book
```

```{r}
bank
```

The cash book has `r big(nrow(cash_book))` entries and the bank statement `r big(nrow(bank))`. Let us compare the closing balances.

```{r}
cb_balance <- opening + sum(cash_book$receipt) - sum(cash_book$payment)
bank_balance <- last(bank$balance)
c(cash_book = cb_balance, bank = bank_balance, difference = bank_balance - cb_balance)
```

The cash book shows ₹`r crore(cb_balance)` crore and the bank ₹`r crore(bank_balance)` crore. The difference is ₹`r inr(bank_balance - cb_balance, 2)`. It is only a net figure. Large items in opposite directions may hide inside it. We must find the items behind it.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip, start with the auditee's own reconciliation

Every office that keeps a bank account must reconcile it, usually every month. So before we match anything, we ask for the office's own reconciliation statements for the year, with their lists of reconciling items. Then we **test** them rather than redo them blindly. Does the statement start from the cash book balance and end at the bank balance? Do the items listed really exist in the records? Are the same items carried month after month? Has anything old quietly disappeared without an entry? The matching in this chapter is the independent check. It is most useful when the office has no reconciliation, when its reconciliation does not close, or when the same items keep appearing.

Get the statement from the bank, or download it in our presence, rather than accept a copy from the office. Altered statements are not unknown. Record a hash of each file received, as in @sec-file-hash. If the statement comes as a PDF, @sec-pdfxl-statement shows how to read it into R and check its running balance.
:::

Before matching, we check that both records are complete, as @sec-jet-complete did for a ledger. One quick check suits a bank statement well. Each balance must equal the previous balance, plus the deposit, less the withdrawal. A missing page, or an altered line, breaks the chain.

```{r}
bank |>
  mutate(expected = lag(balance, default = opening) + deposit - withdrawal) |>
  filter(abs(balance - expected) > 0.005)
```

The chain is unbroken. The cash book has no running balance. For it, we look at the cheque numbers later in the chapter.

## Matching step by step {#sec-recon-steps}

### Preparing the two sides {#sec-recon-prepare}

The two records describe the same events in different words. A receipt in the cash book is a deposit in the bank, and a payment is a withdrawal. So we first bring both to one shape. Each item gets a `direction`, "in" or "out", and a positive `amount`. We also give the columns of each side a prefix, `cb_` or `bs_`, so that we can tell them apart after a join.

The cheque number needs most care. The cash book writes "CHQ 004512", the bank "4512". An exact join on these finds nothing. Let us see how to clean them on a tiny example.

```{r}
refs <- c("CHQ 004512", "CHQ 4512", "004512", "4512", "EP/24-25/0001")
str_extract(refs, "\\d+$")
str_remove(str_extract(refs, "(?<=CHQ )\\d+|^\\d+$"), "^0+")
```

The first try takes the last run of digits. It also turns the e-payment advice into "0001", which is not a cheque number at all. The second try takes digits only after "CHQ ", or a value made only of digits, and then removes the leading zeros. The `(?<=CHQ )` part is a lookbehind, from @sec-regex. Now the four ways of writing cheque 4512 agree, and the advice number becomes `NA`. Here is the full preparation.

```{r}
cb <- cash_book |>
  transmute(cb_id, cb_date = date,
            direction = if_else(receipt > 0, "in", "out"),
            cb_amount = receipt + payment,
            cb_ref = ref,
            cb_chq = str_remove(str_extract(ref, "(?<=^CHQ )\\d+"), "^0+"),
            cb_party = str_to_upper(str_remove(particulars, "^(Paid to|Received from) ")))

bs <- bank |>
  transmute(bs_id, bs_date = date,
            direction = if_else(deposit > 0, "in", "out"),
            bs_amount = deposit + withdrawal,
            narration,
            bs_chq = str_remove(ref, "^0+"),
            bs_party = str_remove(narration, "^(NEFT|RTGS|CLG) (CR|DR) \\S+ |^CHQ PAID \\d+ "))

head(cb, 4)
head(bs, 4)
```

`cb_party` and `bs_party` hold the name of the other party, in capitals on both sides. We will use them to break ties and to group receipts.

### Step 1, exact matches on reference and amount {#sec-recon-exact}

The surest match is the same cheque number, the same direction and the same amount. This is an ordinary equality join, as in @sec-joins, with `join_by()` from @sec-nonequi.

```{r}
step1 <- cb |>
  inner_join(bs, by = join_by(direction, cb_chq == bs_chq, cb_amount == bs_amount),
             na_matches = "never", relationship = "one-to-one")
nrow(step1)
```

Two arguments matter here. By default, `dplyr` treats two missing keys as equal. Every e-payment and receipt has a missing cheque number on both sides, so without `na_matches = "never"` they would all match each other. @sec-joins warned about this trap. And `relationship = "one-to-one"` tells `dplyr` that each item should match at most one item on the other side. If a cheque number and amount appeared twice on either side, the join would stop with an error, instead of quietly matching one item twice.

Step 1 matched `r big(nrow(step1))` cheques. These matches also tell us something useful, which is how long cheques take to clear in this office.

```{r}
step1 |>
  count(days = as.numeric(bs_date - cb_date))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
gaps1 <- as.numeric(step1$bs_date - step1$cb_date)
within5 <- mean(gaps1 <= 5)
within7 <- mean(gaps1 <= 7)
```

`r round(100 * within5)`% of the cheques cleared within five days, and `r round(100 * within7)`% within seven. A few took up to `r max(gaps1)` days. This gives us an evidence-based **window** for the next step. Without a cheque number, a match on amount alone is weaker, so we allow seven days on either side. We note in the working papers how the window was chosen.

Each step removes what it has matched. `anti_join()` from @sec-joins-filter keeps the items not yet matched.

```{r}
cb_left <- cb |> anti_join(step1, by = "cb_id")
bs_left <- bs |> anti_join(step1, by = "bs_id")
c(cash_book = nrow(cb_left), bank = nrow(bs_left))
```

### Step 2, amount within a tolerance and date within a window {#sec-recon-window}

E-payments and receipts have no common reference. We can only match them on direction, amount and date. Two things make this harder. The bank pays e-payments in whole rupees, while the cash book sometimes shows paise. So we allow a **tolerance** of ₹1 on the amount. And the dates differ, so we allow a window of seven days.

Let us see the idea on a tiny example first.

```{r}
t_cb <- tibble(cb_id = c("C1", "C2", "C3"), cb_date = as.Date(c("2024-06-03", "2024-06-10", "2024-06-12")),
               cb_amount = c(12345.60, 8000, 51000))
t_bs <- tibble(bs_id = c("B1", "B2", "B3"), bs_date = as.Date(c("2024-06-04", "2024-06-25", "2024-06-12")),
               bs_amount = c(12346, 8000, 15000))

t_cb |>
  cross_join(t_bs) |>
  filter(abs(bs_amount - cb_amount) <= 1, abs(as.numeric(bs_date - cb_date)) <= 7)
```

`cross_join()` pairs every cash book item with every bank item, and `filter()` keeps the pairs that are close in both amount and date. Only C1 and B1 survive. C2 and B2 have the same amount but are 15 days apart. This works, but a cross join makes every possible pair. Our full data has about two thousand items on each side, which would make about four million pairs. A real year of a large office would make billions.

An **inequality join** does the same work without making every pair first. We add the limits of the window and the tolerance as columns on one side, and use `between()` inside `join_by()`, as in @sec-nonequi.

```{r}
t_limits <- t_cb |>
  mutate(from = cb_date - 7, to = cb_date + 7, low = cb_amount - 1, high = cb_amount + 1)

t_bs |>
  inner_join(t_limits, by = join_by(between(bs_date, from, to), between(bs_amount, low, high)))
```

The answer is the same pair. `between(bs_date, from, to)` keeps bank items dated within the window of a cash book item, and the second `between()` does the same for the amount. Now for the full data. We also require the same direction.

```{r}
window <- 7
tolerance <- 1

cb_limits <- cb_left |>
  mutate(from = cb_date - window, to = cb_date + window,
         low = cb_amount - tolerance, high = cb_amount + tolerance)

candidates <- bs_left |>
  inner_join(cb_limits, by = join_by(direction, between(bs_date, from, to),
                                     between(bs_amount, low, high))) |>
  mutate(day_gap = abs(as.numeric(bs_date - cb_date)),
         amt_diff = round(bs_amount - cb_amount, 2),
         same_party = cb_party == bs_party)
nrow(candidates)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
amb <- candidates |>
  add_count(cb_id, name = "n_cb") |>
  add_count(bs_id, name = "n_bs") |>
  filter(n_cb > 1 | n_bs > 1)
```

There are `r big(nrow(candidates))` candidate pairs, but only `r big(nrow(cb_left))` cash book items. Some items have more than one candidate. Let us count them.

```{r}
candidates |>
  add_count(cb_id, name = "n_cb") |>
  add_count(bs_id, name = "n_bs") |>
  filter(n_cb > 1 | n_bs > 1) |>
  count(cb_amount, sort = TRUE)
```

`r big(n_distinct(amb$cb_id))` cash book items could match more than one bank item. Nearly all are the shop rents. Twelve shops pay ₹15,000 each in the first week of every month, so each rent in the cash book has a dozen candidates in the bank. A plain join would match each of them many times.

### Step 3, one item, one match {#sec-recon-onetoone}

An item may be matched only once. If a bank credit is used to explain two cash book entries, one of those entries is really unmatched, and we have hidden a difference. So from the candidates we must choose one pair for each item. We use a simple rule, and we write it down.

1. Prefer the pair with the closest dates.
2. Among those, prefer the smallest difference in amount.
3. Among those, prefer the pair whose party names agree.

We sort the candidates by these rules and walk down the list. We take a pair only if neither of its items has been taken already. This is called a **greedy** match. Let us see it on two rents.

```{r}
t_cand <- tibble(cb_id    = c("C1", "C1", "C2", "C2"),
                 bs_id    = c("B1", "B2", "B1", "B2"),
                 day_gap  = c(0, 3, 2, 1),
                 amt_diff = 0,
                 same_party = TRUE)

one_to_one <- function(cand) {
  cand <- arrange(cand, day_gap, abs(amt_diff), desc(same_party), cb_id, bs_id)
  used_cb <- character(0)
  used_bs <- character(0)
  keep <- logical(nrow(cand))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(cand))) {
    if (!(cand$cb_id[i] %in% used_cb) && !(cand$bs_id[i] %in% used_bs)) {
      keep[i] <- TRUE
      used_cb <- c(used_cb, cand$cb_id[i])
      used_bs <- c(used_bs, cand$bs_id[i])
    }
  }
  cand[keep, ]
}

one_to_one(t_cand)
```

C1 and B1 are the closest pair, so they are taken first. The next row, C2 with B2, uses neither of them, so it is taken too. The other two rows are skipped, because their items are already used. The last two keys of the sort, `cb_id` and `bs_id`, only make sure that the result is the same every time we run it. Now the full candidates.

```{r}
step3 <- one_to_one(candidates)
nrow(step3)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rnd <- step3 |> filter(amt_diff != 0)
diff_party <- step3 |> filter(!same_party)
```

Steps 2 and 3 together matched `r big(nrow(step3))` items. Two checks on the result are worth a minute. First, how many pairs differ in amount?

```{r}
step3 |>
  filter(amt_diff != 0) |>
  summarise(pairs = n(), net = sum(amt_diff), largest = max(abs(amt_diff)))
```

`r nrow(rnd)` pairs differ, by at most ₹`r inr(max(abs(rnd$amt_diff)), 2)`. They are the e-payments the bank rounded. Together they make a net difference of ₹`r inr(abs(sum(rnd$amt_diff)), 2)`, which will appear in the reconciliation statement. A tolerance does not make a difference disappear. It only lets us pair the items, and the difference must still be explained. Second, do the party names agree?

```{r}
step3 |>
  filter(!same_party) |>
  count(cb_party, bs_party)
```

`r nrow(diff_party)` pairs have different names. All of them are bank charges and interest, which the cash book describes in its own words. Every other pair has the same party on both sides. Without the third rule, the rents of different shops paid on the same day could have been paired with each other. The totals would not change, but the working papers would show the wrong shop.

```{r}
cb_left2 <- cb_left |> anti_join(step3, by = "cb_id")
bs_left2 <- bs_left |> anti_join(step3, by = "bs_id")
c(cash_book = nrow(cb_left2), bank = nrow(bs_left2))
```

### Step 4, one credit for several receipts {#sec-recon-combn}

Sometimes one bank item settles several cash book items. A party pays three bills by one transfer, and the cashier writes three receipts. No single receipt matches the credit, so steps 1 to 3 cannot find it. We must look for a **combination** of receipts whose total equals the credit.

Base R's `combn()` lists all combinations of a given size. Let us find which receipts of one party add up to a credit of ₹88,870.

```{r}
receipts <- c(42350, 18920, 27600, 9100)
combn(4, 2)
combn(4, 3)
```

Each column is one combination of positions. `combn(4, 2)` gives the six pairs, and `combn(4, 3)` the four triples. We sum the amounts in each column and look for the target.

```{r}
pos <- combn(4, 3)
sums <- colSums(matrix(receipts[pos], nrow = 3))
sums
pos[, sums == 88870]
```

The first, second and third receipts add up to the credit. The function below tries pairs first, then triples, and returns the positions of the first combination within the tolerance.

```{r}
find_combo <- function(target, amounts, max_size = 3, tolerance = 1) {
  if (length(amounts) < 2) return(NULL)
  for (k in 2:min(max_size, length(amounts))) {
    pos <- combn(length(amounts), k)
    sums <- colSums(matrix(amounts[pos], nrow = k))
    hit <- which(abs(sums - target) <= tolerance)
    if (length(hit) > 0) return(pos[, hit[1]])
  }
  NULL
}

find_combo(88870, receipts)
```

The number of combinations grows very fast. Ten items have `r choose(10, 3)` triples, but forty items have `r big(choose(40, 3))` triples and `r big(choose(40, 5))` groups of five. A search over all receipts of the year would never finish. Worse, with so many combinations, some would add up to the target by pure chance. So we keep the search **small**. We look only at receipts of the same party, within the window before the credit, and only at groups of two or three.

```{r}
credits <- bs_left2 |> filter(direction == "in")
found <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(credits))) {
  b <- credits[i, ]
  pool <- cb_left2 |>
    filter(direction == "in", cb_party == b$bs_party,
           cb_date >= b$bs_date - window, cb_date <= b$bs_date)
  pick <- find_combo(b$bs_amount, pool$cb_amount)
  if (!is.null(pick)) {
    found[[length(found) + 1]] <- tibble(bs_id = b$bs_id, cb_id = pool$cb_id[pick])
  }
}
step4 <- bind_rows(found)

step4 |>
  left_join(select(cb, cb_id, cb_date, cb_ref, cb_party, cb_amount), by = "cb_id") |>
  left_join(select(bs, bs_id, bs_date, bs_amount), by = "bs_id")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
s4 <- step4 |>
  left_join(select(cb, cb_id, cb_party, cb_amount), by = "cb_id") |>
  left_join(select(bs, bs_id, bs_amount), by = "bs_id") |>
  summarise(n = n(), bs_amount = first(bs_amount), .by = c(bs_id, cb_party))
```

Two credits are explained. One credit of ₹`r inr(s4$bs_amount[s4$n == 3])` from `r str_to_title(s4$cb_party[s4$n == 3])` settles `r s4$n[s4$n == 3]` receipts, and one of ₹`r inr(s4$bs_amount[s4$n == 2])` from `r str_to_title(s4$cb_party[s4$n == 2])` settles `r s4$n[s4$n == 2]`. The same function works the other way round, for one cash book entry against several bank items. That happens when a payment is split by the bank, or when the office enters a day's deposits as one total.

```{r}
cb_left3 <- cb_left2 |> anti_join(step4, by = "cb_id")
bs_left3 <- bs_left2 |> anti_join(step4, by = "bs_id")
c(cash_book = nrow(cb_left3), bank = nrow(bs_left3))
```

### Step 5, references typed wrongly {#sec-recon-fuzzy}

Some cheques are still unmatched on both sides. A cheque matches in step 1 only if its number is typed correctly. If the number is wrong, the cheque can still match in step 2 on amount and date, but only if it cleared within the window. A cheque with a wrong number that was presented late escapes both steps. For these, we compare the cheque numbers with a **string distance**, as in @sec-strsim.

The optimal string alignment distance, method `"osa"`, counts the changes needed to turn one string into another. A change is one character inserted, deleted or replaced, or two neighbouring characters swapped.

```{r}
stringdist(c("4103", "4103", "4103", "4103"), c("4103", "4013", "4108", "5262"), method = "osa")
```

A swap of two digits, or one wrong digit, gives a distance of 1. So we pair the remaining cheques that have the same direction and amount. We keep the pairs whose numbers are at distance 1 or less, and whose dates are not too far apart.

```{r}
step5 <- cb_left3 |>
  filter(!is.na(cb_chq)) |>
  inner_join(filter(bs_left3, !is.na(bs_chq)), by = join_by(direction, cb_amount == bs_amount)) |>
  mutate(ref_dist = stringdist(cb_chq, bs_chq, method = "osa"),
         day_gap = as.numeric(bs_date - cb_date), amt_diff = 0, same_party = cb_party == bs_party) |>
  filter(ref_dist <= 1, day_gap >= 0, day_gap <= 30) |>
  one_to_one()

step5 |>
  select(cb_ref, bs_chq, cb_amount, cb_date, bs_date, ref_dist)
```

Step 5 finds `r nrow(step5)` cheques. In each, the cash book number differs from the bank's by one change, the amount is the same, and the bank paid it `r min(step5$day_gap)` to `r max(step5$day_gap)` days later. They are typing errors in the cash book, and the office should correct them. Note that we required the amounts to be equal. Allowing both a different number and a different amount would pair cheques that have nothing to do with each other.

```{r}
cb_left4 <- cb_left3 |> anti_join(step5, by = "cb_id")
bs_left4 <- bs_left3 |> anti_join(step5, by = "bs_id")
c(cash_book = nrow(cb_left4), bank = nrow(bs_left4))
```

### Same reference, different amount {#sec-recon-transpose}

One last check is the reverse of step 5. Are there cheques with the **same** number on both sides but a different amount?

```{r}
same_ref <- cb_left4 |>
  inner_join(bs_left4, by = join_by(direction, cb_chq == bs_chq), na_matches = "never") |>
  mutate(difference = cb_amount - bs_amount, divisible_by_9 = difference %% 9 == 0)

same_ref |>
  select(cb_ref, cb_date, bs_date, cb_amount, bs_amount, difference, divisible_by_9)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
tr <- same_ref[1, ]
```

Cheque `r tr$cb_ref` is entered in the cash book as ₹`r inr(tr$cb_amount)`, but the bank paid ₹`r inr(tr$bs_amount)`. The difference, ₹`r inr(tr$difference)`, is divisible by 9. This is the mark of a **transposition**, two digits written in the wrong order. Swapping two digits always changes a number by a multiple of 9. Here 54,320 and 45,320 differ only in the order of the first two digits. The bank paid what the cheque said, so the cash book has overstated the payment by ₹`r inr(tr$difference)`. It is a permanent difference. The office must correct its cash book.

```{r}
cb_final <- cb_left4 |> filter(!cb_id %in% same_ref$cb_id)
bs_final <- bs_left4 |> filter(!bs_id %in% same_ref$bs_id)
```

::: callout-warning
## Caution, a match is not proof

A matched pair may still be wrong. The tolerance and the window let us pair items that are close, and two unrelated items can be close by chance. Two errors can also cancel. A payment left out of the cash book and a receipt left out in the same week, of similar amounts, leave the totals correct. A match says only that the two records agree on that item. It does not say that the payment was proper.

The tolerance, the window and the size of combinations are our choices, and different choices give different results. Choose them from the data, as we chose the window from the clearing times in step 1. Keep them as small as the data allows. State them in the working papers, with the number of items matched at each step, so that a reviewer can repeat the work.
:::

Let us count what each step matched.

```{r}
tibble(step = c("1. Same cheque number and amount", "2 and 3. Amount and date, one to one",
                "4. Combinations of receipts", "5. Cheque numbers typed wrongly",
                "Same number, different amount"),
       cash_book = c(nrow(step1), nrow(step3), n_distinct(step4$cb_id), nrow(step5), nrow(same_ref)),
       bank      = c(nrow(step1), nrow(step3), n_distinct(step4$bs_id), nrow(step5), nrow(same_ref)))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
matched_cb <- nrow(cb) - nrow(cb_final)
```

`r big(matched_cb)` of the `r big(nrow(cb))` cash book entries are accounted for. `r nrow(cb_final)` remain in the cash book, and `r nrow(bs_final)` in the bank statement.

## Audit use case, bank statement and cash book {#sec-recon-bank}

We now turn the leftovers into a reconciliation. We classify each item as a timing or a permanent difference, age it, value it, check whether the timing items really cleared, and present the statement.

### What is left on each side {#sec-recon-left}

We put the leftovers of both sides in one table, with a column saying which side each comes from.

```{r}
year_end <- as.Date("2025-03-31")

left <- bind_rows(
  cb_final |> transmute(side = "Cash book", id = cb_id, date = cb_date, direction, amount = cb_amount,
                        detail = paste(cb_ref, cb_party)),
  bs_final |> transmute(side = "Bank", id = bs_id, date = bs_date, direction, amount = bs_amount,
                        detail = narration)) |>
  mutate(age_days = as.numeric(year_end - date),
         age = cut(age_days, breaks = c(-Inf, 30, 90, 180, Inf),
                   labels = c("Up to 30 days", "31 to 90 days", "91 to 180 days", "Over 180 days")),
         class = case_when(
           side == "Cash book" & direction == "out" & age_days <= 90 ~ "Timing, payment not yet debited by bank",
           side == "Cash book" & direction == "out"                  ~ "Stale, cheque over three months old",
           side == "Cash book" & direction == "in"                   ~ "Timing, deposit not yet credited by bank",
           side == "Bank" & str_detect(detail, "CHGS")               ~ "Permanent, bank charges not in cash book",
           side == "Bank" & str_detect(detail, "^INT CR")            ~ "Permanent, interest not in cash book",
           side == "Bank" & direction == "out"                       ~ "Permanent, withdrawal not in cash book",
           .default = "Permanent, other"))

left |>
  summarise(items = n(), amount = sum(amount), oldest_days = max(age_days), .by = c(side, class)) |>
  arrange(side, class)
```

`cut()` puts each age into a band. `case_when()` gives each item a class, in the order written. A cash book payment is timing if it is less than three months old, and stale if it is older. Let us look at the age bands across both sides.

```{r}
left |>
  count(age, side) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = side, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
old <- left |> filter(age_days > 30) |> arrange(desc(age_days))
unauth <- left |> filter(class == "Permanent, withdrawal not in cash book")
chg_left <- left |> filter(class == "Permanent, bank charges not in cash book")
int_left <- left |> filter(class == "Permanent, interest not in cash book")
dit_left <- left |> filter(class == "Timing, deposit not yet credited by bank")
upc_left <- left |> filter(class == "Timing, payment not yet debited by bank")
stale_left <- left |> filter(class == "Stale, cheque over three months old")
```

Most items are less than a month old, as timing items should be. The old ones need attention. Here they are.

```{r}
left |>
  filter(age_days > 30) |>
  arrange(desc(age_days)) |>
  select(side, date, age_days, amount, detail, class)
```

These are the items for the audit. Let us take them one by one.

- **The self cheque.** On `r fdate(unauth$date)` the bank paid ₹`r lakh(unauth$amount)` lakh in cash on cheque `r str_extract(unauth$detail, "\\d+$")`, drawn to "self". The cash book has no entry for it. It is the most serious item in the reconciliation.
- **The cheque that never reached the bank.** A cheque of ₹`r inr(max(stale_left$amount))` to `r str_to_title(str_remove(stale_left$detail[stale_left$amount == max(stale_left$amount)], "^CHQ \\d+ "))`, dated `r fdate(stale_left$date[stale_left$amount == max(stale_left$amount)])`, has not been presented in `r stale_left$age_days[stale_left$amount == max(stale_left$amount)]` days. A contractor does not usually forget a cheque of this size. Perhaps it was cancelled and the cash book never reversed it. Perhaps it was never issued, and the payment in the cash book was a way to take money out of the books.
- **The stale cheque.** A cheque of ₹`r inr(stale_left$amount[stale_left$amount == min(stale_left$amount)])`, dated `r fdate(stale_left$date[stale_left$amount == min(stale_left$amount)])`, is over six months old. The bank will not pay it now. It should be cancelled and written back.
- **Bank charges.** `r nrow(chg_left)` charges of January to March, ₹`r inr(sum(chg_left$amount), 2)` in all, are not in the cash book. They are small and genuine, but the cash book is wrong until they are entered. They are left from `r fdate(min(chg_left$date))`, so the office stopped entering charges after December.

Two other permanent items are recent. The interest of ₹`r inr(int_left$amount)` credited on 31 March is not in the cash book. Interest earned on scheme funds is often required to be returned to the government or used only as directed. The auditor checks what the scheme's instructions say, and whether the interest of September was dealt with correctly. And the transposition error of ₹`r inr(tr$difference)` must be corrected.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip, the cheque series

The self cheque came from the society's own cheque book. If the cash book records every cheque issued, there must be a gap in its series where that cheque should be. @sec-gaps shows how to find gaps in a series of numbers. Here we simply look at the neighbours.

```{r}
unauth_no <- as.integer(str_extract(unauth$detail, "\\d+$"))
cb |>
  filter(as.integer(cb_chq) %in% (unauth_no + -2:2)) |>
  select(cb_id, cb_date, cb_ref, cb_party, cb_amount)
```

The cheques before and after it were issued on nearby days and entered normally. The cheque issue register and the cheque book counterfoil will show who signed this one and who took the cash.
:::

### Did the timing items clear? {#sec-recon-subsequent}

We have called `r nrow(upc_left)` payments and `r nrow(dit_left)` deposits timing differences. That is only our expectation. The way to test it is to look at the next bank statement. Each of them should appear there within days. This is the **subsequent clearance** test. We match the timing items against the April statement, by cheque number where there is one, and otherwise by amount within the tolerance.

```{r}
apr <- bank_apr |>
  transmute(apr_date = date, apr_chq = str_remove(ref, "^0+"), apr_amount = deposit + withdrawal,
            direction = if_else(deposit > 0, "in", "out"))

timing <- left |>
  filter(side == "Cash book") |>
  left_join(select(cb, cb_id, cb_chq), by = join_by(id == cb_id))

cleared_chq <- timing |>
  filter(!is.na(cb_chq)) |>
  left_join(apr, by = join_by(direction, cb_chq == apr_chq, amount == apr_amount), na_matches = "never")

cleared_other <- timing |>
  filter(is.na(cb_chq)) |>
  left_join(apr |> filter(is.na(apr_chq)) |> mutate(low = apr_amount - 1, high = apr_amount + 1),
            by = join_by(direction, between(amount, low, high)))

cleared <- bind_rows(cleared_chq, cleared_other) |>
  rename(cleared_on = apr_date)

cleared |>
  summarise(items = n(), cleared = sum(!is.na(cleared_on)), .by = class)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
not_cleared <- cleared |> filter(is.na(cleared_on))
dup_check <- cleared |> count(id) |> filter(n > 1)
last_clear <- max(cleared$cleared_on, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Every timing item cleared in April, the last on `r fdate(last_clear)`. They were genuine. The `r nrow(not_cleared)` items that did not clear are the two stale cheques. `r if (nrow(dup_check) == 0) "Each item found exactly one April entry." else "Some items found more than one April entry, and need a closer look."` A real audit would look further, at May and June, and at the reconciliations of those months.

### The reconciliation statement {#sec-recon-statement}

We can now present the statement in the familiar form. It starts from the balance as per the cash book. It adds the items that make the bank balance higher and takes away those that make it lower. It should end at the balance as per the bank.

Each kind of item moves the bank balance in a known direction. A payment in the cash book that the bank has not yet made leaves more money in the bank, so it is added. A deposit the bank has not yet credited is taken away. Interest credited by the bank only is added, and charges and withdrawals by the bank only are taken away. The transposition error made the cash book payment larger than the bank's, so the difference is added. The rounding differences are added or taken away according to their net sign.

```{r}
rounding_net <- sum(step3$amt_diff * if_else(step3$direction == "out", -1, 1))

recon <- tribble(
  ~particulars,                                                    ~amount,
  "Balance as per cash book",                                      cb_balance,
  "Add, cheques and e-payments issued but not yet debited by bank", sum(upc_left$amount),
  "Add, stale cheques not yet presented",                          sum(stale_left$amount),
  "Add, interest credited by bank, not in cash book",             sum(int_left$amount),
  "Add, excess payment entered in cash book (transposition)",      tr$difference,
  "Less, deposits not yet credited by bank",                       -sum(dit_left$amount),
  "Less, bank charges not in cash book",                           -sum(chg_left$amount),
  "Less, cash withdrawn on self cheque, not in cash book",         -sum(unauth$amount),
  "Add or less, net rounding of e-payments by bank",               rounding_net
)

recon_check <- sum(recon$amount)
c(computed = recon_check, as_per_bank = bank_balance, difference = round(recon_check - bank_balance, 2))
```

The computed balance agrees with the bank to the paisa. The reconciliation **closes**. Every rupee of the difference between the two records is explained. Here is the statement as it would go into the working papers.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recon-statement
#| tbl-cap: "Bank reconciliation statement of the District Health Society, Keshavnagar, at 31 March 2025"
recon |>
  mutate(`Amount (₹)` = paste0(if_else(amount < 0, "(", ""), inr(amount, 2), if_else(amount < 0, ")", ""))) |>
  select(Particulars = particulars, `Amount (₹)`) |>
  add_row(Particulars = "Balance as per bank statement", `Amount (₹)` = inr(recon_check, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", "r"))
```

Amounts in brackets are taken away. A statement that closes is necessary, but it is not the end. It is easy to make a statement close with a balancing figure called "difference under investigation". If such a line appears in the auditee's statements, month after month, it is itself a finding.

### What the auditor does next

1. **The self cheque.** Get the cheque from the bank, with its image and the signatures on it. Check the cheque issue register and the counterfoil. Find out who withdrew the cash, and whether it was ever brought into the cash book. Treat it as a possible misappropriation until it is explained, and report it at once to the head of the office.
2. **The cheque never presented.** Ask for the bill, the sanction and the contractor's acknowledgement. Ask the contractor, in writing, whether the cheque was received. If it was cancelled, see that the cash book is reversed. If no work was done for it, the payment was not real.
3. **The stale cheque.** See that it is cancelled and written back, and that the supplier is paid afresh if still owed.
4. **Charges and interest.** See that they are entered, and that the interest is dealt with as the scheme's instructions require.
5. **The errors.** See that the transposition and the four wrong cheque numbers are corrected in the cash book.
6. **The controls.** Ask why the office's own reconciliations did not bring out these items. A monthly reconciliation done properly would have shown the self cheque in January.

## Audit use case, input tax credit against suppliers' returns {#sec-recon-itc}

Under GST, a business pays tax on its sales. It may reduce that tax by the tax it has already paid on its purchases. This reduction is called **input tax credit**. Each month the business files a summary return, **GSTR-3B**, in which it pays its tax and claims its credit. Its suppliers, in their own returns, report every invoice they issued to it. From these reports the GST system prepares for the business a monthly statement, **GSTR-2B**, listing the invoices on which credit is available.

So two records exist. The business's purchase register shows the credit it claimed, invoice by invoice. The GSTR-2B shows the invoices its suppliers reported. Broadly, credit claimed on an invoice that no supplier reported is not supported. It is the main risk, because a fake invoice from a supplier who files nothing gives credit that was never paid as tax by anyone. The rules on such claims have changed over time and have exceptions, so the treatment of each difference should be checked against the GST law in force. Our task is the reconciliation itself.

Our business is an imaginary food processing company, Keshav Agro Foods Private Limited. Its purchase register `purchases` has one row per invoice claimed in 2024-25. `gstr2b` has one row per invoice reported by its suppliers. The firm names and GSTINs are made up, but each GSTIN is built with a correct check character, using the function of @sec-checkdigits. These cases are planted.

1. **Credit on invoices that suppliers never reported.** All the invoices of one supplier, and six invoices of other suppliers.
2. **Invoice numbers written differently.** Three suppliers write "INV-0012" in their returns, where the register has "INV/24-25/0012".
3. **Small rounding differences.** The company rounded the tax on some invoices to the rupee.
4. **An invoice claimed twice.** The same invoice appears in two months of the register.
5. **A GSTIN that fails the check.** One invoice is entered under a GSTIN with a typing error.

Some invoices were also reported late by their suppliers, a month after the invoice.

```{r}
gst_chars <- c(0:9, LETTERS)

gstin_check_char <- function(first14) {
  v <- match(strsplit(first14, "")[[1]], gst_chars) - 1
  p <- v * rep(c(1, 2), 7)
  total <- sum(p %/% 36 + p %% 36)
  gst_chars[((36 - total %% 36) %% 36) + 1]
}

gstin_valid <- function(x) {
  x <- str_to_upper(str_remove_all(x, "\\s"))
  map_lgl(x, function(g) {
    if (is.na(g) || !str_detect(g, "^[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z][1-9A-Z]Z[0-9A-Z]$")) {
      return(FALSE)
    }
    gstin_check_char(str_sub(g, 1, 14)) == str_sub(g, 15, 15)
  })
}
```

These are the two functions of @sec-regex-validate, repeated here so that the chapter runs on its own.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the purchase register and the GSTR-2B"
set.seed(3125)
names_sup <- c("Aarav Packaging Industries", "Bhagwati Grain Traders", "Chandan Spices", "Dhruv Cold Chain",
               "Ekta Plastics", "Falgun Agro Inputs", "Ganga Edible Oils", "Hari Om Logistics",
               "Indu Corrugators", "Jagdamba Pulses", "Kamdhenu Dairy Products", "Laxmi Labels",
               "Madhav Machinery Works", "Nandini Salt Works", "Omkar Chemicals", "Pushpak Transport",
               "Radhe Flour Mills", "Sarthak Engineering", "Tulsi Tea Company", "Umang Fuels",
               "Vardhman Agri Traders", "Yamuna Sugar Agencies", "Zeal Electricals", "Shubh Laminates",
               "Kesar Food Colours", "Anmol Jute Bags", "Sagar Cartons", "Prabhat Fasteners")
make_gstin <- function(state, name) {
  pan <- paste0(paste(sample(LETTERS, 3, TRUE), collapse = ""), sample(c("F", "C"), 1), substr(name, 1, 1),
                sprintf("%04d", sample(1000:9999, 1)), sample(LETTERS, 1))
  first14 <- paste0(state, pan, "1Z")
  paste0(first14, gstin_check_char(first14))
}
suppliers <- tibble(supplier_name = names_sup,
                    state = sample(c("09", "27", "07", "23", "08"), length(names_sup), TRUE)) |>
  mutate(supplier_gstin = map2_chr(state, supplier_name, make_gstin),
         prefix = if_else(row_number() %in% c(3, 9, 17), "INV",
                          map_chr(str_split(supplier_name, " "), \(w) paste(substr(w, 1, 1), collapse = ""))))

n_inv <- 640
inv <- tibble(sup = sample(nrow(suppliers), n_inv, TRUE, prob = rep(c(3, 2, 1, 1), 7)),
              invoice_date = sort(sample(seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-31"), by = "day"),
                                         n_inv, TRUE))) |>
  mutate(supplier_name = suppliers$supplier_name[sup], supplier_gstin = suppliers$supplier_gstin[sup],
         prefix = suppliers$prefix[sup]) |>
  mutate(seq_no = row_number() * 3 + sample(0:2, n(), TRUE), .by = sup) |>
  mutate(invoice_no = sprintf("%s/24-25/%04d", prefix, seq_no),
         taxable_value = round(rlnorm(n_inv, log(85000), 1), 2),
         rate = sample(c(5, 12, 18), n_inv, TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.2, 0.3)),
         tax = round(taxable_value * rate / 100, 2),
         period = floor_date(invoice_date, "month"))

# The suppliers' side. Three suppliers write their numbers in a short form.
g2b <- inv |>
  mutate(invoice_no = if_else(prefix == "INV", sprintf("INV-%04d", seq_no), invoice_no),
         period = if_else(row_number() %in% sample(n(), 9), period %m+% months(1), period))
# Planted. One supplier reports nothing, and six other invoices are not reported
vardhman <- inv$supplier_name == "Vardhman Agri Traders"
missing6 <- sample(which(!vardhman), 6)
g2b <- g2b[-c(which(vardhman), missing6), ]
# Invoices reported by suppliers but not claimed by the company
g2b_extra <- inv[!vardhman, ] |> slice_sample(n = 5) |>
  mutate(seq_no = seq_no + 5000, invoice_no = sprintf("%s/24-25/%04d", prefix, seq_no),
         invoice_no = if_else(prefix == "INV", sprintf("INV-%04d", seq_no), invoice_no))
g2b <- bind_rows(g2b, g2b_extra)

# The company's side
pr <- inv
rnd <- sample(which(!vardhman), 22)
pr$tax[rnd] <- round(pr$tax[rnd])                                   # Planted. Tax rounded to the rupee
dup <- sample(setdiff(which(!vardhman & inv$period <= as.Date("2024-09-01")), missing6), 1)
pr <- bind_rows(pr, pr[dup, ] |> mutate(period = period %m+% months(2)))  # Planted. Claimed twice
typo <- sample(setdiff(which(!vardhman), c(missing6, dup)), 1)
g <- pr$supplier_gstin[typo]                                         # Planted. GSTIN typed wrongly
pr$supplier_gstin[typo] <- paste0(substr(g, 1, 8), if_else(substr(g, 9, 9) == "8", "3", "8"), substr(g, 10, 15))

purchases <- pr |>
  arrange(period, invoice_date) |>
  transmute(pr_id = sprintf("PR%04d", row_number()), claimed_in = period, supplier_gstin, supplier_name,
            invoice_no, invoice_date, taxable_value, tax)
gstr2b <- g2b |>
  arrange(period, invoice_date) |>
  transmute(return_period = period, supplier_gstin, supplier_name = str_to_upper(supplier_name),
            invoice_no, invoice_date, taxable_value, tax)

rm(names_sup, make_gstin, suppliers, n_inv, inv, g2b, vardhman, missing6, g2b_extra, pr, rnd, dup, typo, g)
```

```{r}
purchases
gstr2b
```

```{r}
#| include: false
itc_claimed <- sum(purchases$tax)
itc_avail <- sum(gstr2b$tax)
```

The company claimed ₹`r lakh(itc_claimed)` lakh of credit on `r nrow(purchases)` invoices. Its suppliers reported invoices carrying ₹`r lakh(itc_avail)` lakh. The difference, ₹`r lakh(itc_claimed - itc_avail)` lakh, is again a net figure. Let us first compare the two month by month, as a quick view.

```{r}
monthly <- full_join(
  purchases |> summarise(claimed = sum(tax), .by = claimed_in) |> rename(month = claimed_in),
  gstr2b |> summarise(available = sum(tax), .by = return_period) |> rename(month = return_period),
  by = "month") |>
  mutate(across(c(claimed, available), \(x) coalesce(x, 0)),
         excess = round(claimed - available, 2)) |>
  arrange(month)
monthly
```

```{r}
#| include: false
neg_months <- sum(monthly$excess < 0)
```

Most months show an excess claim, but `r if (neg_months == 1) "one month shows" else paste(neg_months, "months show")` less claimed than available. A monthly view mixes up timing and real differences. An invoice reported late by its supplier makes one month look short and the next look long. Only the invoice-level match can separate them.

### Checking the GSTINs

The supplier's GSTIN is the key that ties the two sides together. So we check it first.

```{r}
purchases |>
  mutate(valid = gstin_valid(supplier_gstin)) |>
  filter(!valid) |>
  select(pr_id, supplier_gstin, supplier_name, invoice_no, tax)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bad <- purchases |> filter(!gstin_valid(supplier_gstin))
```

One invoice carries a GSTIN that fails the check character. Is it a typing error, or a supplier who does not exist? `amatch()` from `stringdist`, met in @sec-strsim, finds the closest GSTIN among those the suppliers reported.

```{r}
reported <- unique(gstr2b$supplier_gstin)
closest <- reported[amatch(bad$supplier_gstin, reported, method = "osa", maxDist = 1)]
closest
gstr2b |>
  filter(supplier_gstin == closest) |>
  distinct(supplier_gstin, supplier_name)
```

The closest valid GSTIN differs by one character and belongs to the supplier of the same name. It is a typing error in the register, and we correct it for matching. Had no close GSTIN been found, the invoice would join the unsupported claims below.

```{r}
purchases_fixed <- purchases |>
  mutate(supplier_gstin = if_else(pr_id %in% bad$pr_id, closest, supplier_gstin))
```

### Matching invoice by invoice

Within one supplier, the invoice number identifies the invoice. But three suppliers write their numbers in a short form in the GSTR-2B. We clean them as we cleaned the cheque numbers, keeping the last run of digits as a number.

```{r}
str_extract(c("INV/24-25/0012", "INV-0012", "RFM/24-25/0012"), "\\d+$") |> as.integer()
```

Now we add this key, called `inv_key`, on both sides. Before joining, we look for invoices claimed more than once, as in @sec-dup.

```{r}
pr_key <- purchases_fixed |> mutate(inv_key = as.integer(str_extract(invoice_no, "\\d+$")))
g2_key <- gstr2b |> mutate(inv_key = as.integer(str_extract(invoice_no, "\\d+$")))

pr_key |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(supplier_gstin, inv_key)) |>
  select(pr_id, claimed_in, supplier_name, invoice_no, invoice_date, tax)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
twice <- pr_key |> filter(n() > 1, .by = c(supplier_gstin, inv_key))
```

Invoice `r twice$invoice_no[1]` of `r twice$supplier_name[1]` was claimed in `r format(twice$claimed_in[1], "%B %Y")` and again in `r format(twice$claimed_in[2], "%B %Y")`. The second claim, ₹`r inr(twice$tax[2], 2)`, has no basis whatever the GSTR-2B says. We keep the first claim for matching and set the second aside. The GSTR-2B should be checked for duplicates in the same way. Now the match. Each invoice should appear once on each side, so we use `relationship = "one-to-one"` again.

```{r}
pr_first <- pr_key |> filter(row_number() == 1, .by = c(supplier_gstin, inv_key))
pr_second <- pr_key |> anti_join(pr_first, by = "pr_id")

itc <- pr_first |>
  left_join(select(g2_key, supplier_gstin, inv_key, return_period, g2b_no = invoice_no, g2b_tax = tax),
            by = join_by(supplier_gstin, inv_key), relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(tax_diff = round(tax - g2b_tax, 2),
         status = case_when(
           is.na(g2b_tax)       ~ "Not reported by supplier",
           tax_diff == 0        ~ "Matched exactly",
           abs(tax_diff) <= 1   ~ "Matched within Re 1",
           .default             = "Matched, tax differs"))

itc |>
  summarise(invoices = n(), credit_claimed = sum(tax), excess = sum(tax - coalesce(g2b_tax, 0)),
            .by = status)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
st <- itc |> summarise(n = n(), excess = sum(tax - coalesce(g2b_tax, 0)), .by = status)
nr <- itc |> filter(status == "Not reported by supplier")
nr_sup <- nr |> summarise(invoices = n(), tax = sum(tax), .by = supplier_name) |> arrange(desc(tax))
diff_no <- itc |> filter(!is.na(g2b_no), invoice_no != g2b_no)
late_rep <- itc |> filter(!is.na(return_period), return_period != claimed_in)
```

`r st$n[st$status == "Matched exactly"]` invoices match exactly. `r st$n[st$status == "Matched within Re 1"]` match within a rupee, where the company rounded the tax, and the net difference on them is only ₹`r inr(abs(st$excess[st$status == "Matched within Re 1"]), 2)`. `r nrow(diff_no)` of the matched invoices had numbers written differently on the two sides, and would have been missed by a join on the raw number. `r nrow(late_rep)` invoices were matched although their supplier reported them a month late. They explain the months that looked short.

`r nrow(nr)` invoices, carrying credit of ₹`r lakh(sum(nr$tax))` lakh, were never reported by any supplier. Let us see whose they are.

```{r}
nr |>
  summarise(invoices = n(), credit = sum(tax), first = min(invoice_date), last = max(invoice_date),
            .by = c(supplier_gstin, supplier_name)) |>
  arrange(desc(credit))
```

`r nr_sup$supplier_name[1]` accounts for `r nr_sup$invoices[1]` invoices and ₹`r lakh(nr_sup$tax[1])` lakh. Not one of its invoices appears in the GSTR-2B. A supplier that reports nothing for a whole year may have stopped filing, may have had its registration cancelled, or may never have supplied anything. The others are one or two invoices each, of suppliers who reported their other sales. They may be omissions by the supplier, which the company should take up, or invoices that do not exist.

Finally the reverse direction. Are there invoices reported by suppliers that the company did not claim?

```{r}
g2_key |>
  anti_join(pr_first, by = join_by(supplier_gstin, inv_key)) |>
  select(return_period, supplier_name, invoice_no, tax)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
unclaimed <- g2_key |> anti_join(pr_first, by = join_by(supplier_gstin, inv_key))
```

`r nrow(unclaimed)` invoices with credit of ₹`r inr(sum(unclaimed$tax))` were reported but not claimed. This does not harm the revenue. It may be credit the company has chosen not to claim, or purchases that are not in its register at all. The second is worth asking about, because unrecorded purchases can mean unrecorded sales.

### What the auditor does next

1. **Quantify the unsupported credit.** Credit on invoices never reported, ₹`r lakh(sum(nr$tax))` lakh, and the second claim of the duplicate invoice, ₹`r inr(twice$tax[2], 2)`. Check each against the GST law in force, including any conditions that allow credit in special cases.
2. **Look at the supplier that reported nothing.** Check its registration status, its returns and its tax payments on the GST system. Ask the company for the purchase orders, goods received notes, transport documents and payment proofs for its invoices.
3. **Follow up the single invoices.** Ask whether the company has taken up the omissions with its suppliers, and whether the invoices were reported later.
4. **Ignore what is explained.** Rounding differences and invoices reported a month late are timing or trivial. Record them, but do not report them.
5. **Report data errors as such.** The wrong GSTIN and the different invoice formats are weaknesses in the company's records, not losses of revenue.

::: callout-warning
## Caution, business and personal data

Purchase registers, GSTINs and bank statements are confidential. A bank statement of an office can also hold the names and account details of staff and beneficiaries, and a GSTIN contains the PAN of the business or its proprietor. Keep such files on audit systems, share only what each finding needs, and mask identifiers in reports and presentations. @sec-privacy shows how.
:::

## Cross-verification of aggregates, department and treasury {#sec-recon-treasury}

Sometimes we do not have item-level data on both sides, or we do not need it. A department keeps its own record of expenditure. The treasury, which passes and pays the bills, keeps another. The two should agree each month for each head of account, and departments are usually required to reconcile their figures with the treasury's. Here the comparison is of totals, by month and head.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the department's and the treasury's figures"
set.seed(77)
heads <- c("Salaries", "Office expenses", "Medicines", "Minor works", "Grants to hospitals")
dept_exp <- expand_grid(month = seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-03-01"), by = "month"),
                        head = heads) |>
  mutate(amount = round(c(4.2e7, 1.8e6, 9.5e6, 3.4e6, 1.2e7)[match(head, heads)] * runif(n(), 0.85, 1.15), -2))
treasury_exp <- dept_exp
# Planted. A bill classified as minor works by the department, office expenses by the treasury
nov <- treasury_exp$month == as.Date("2024-11-01")
treasury_exp$amount[nov & treasury_exp$head == "Minor works"] <-
  treasury_exp$amount[nov & treasury_exp$head == "Minor works"] - 310000
treasury_exp$amount[nov & treasury_exp$head == "Office expenses"] <-
  treasury_exp$amount[nov & treasury_exp$head == "Office expenses"] + 310000
# Planted. A medicine bill booked by the department in September, passed by the treasury in October
treasury_exp$amount[treasury_exp$month == as.Date("2024-09-01") & treasury_exp$head == "Medicines"] <-
  treasury_exp$amount[treasury_exp$month == as.Date("2024-09-01") & treasury_exp$head == "Medicines"] - 475000
treasury_exp$amount[treasury_exp$month == as.Date("2024-10-01") & treasury_exp$head == "Medicines"] <-
  treasury_exp$amount[treasury_exp$month == as.Date("2024-10-01") & treasury_exp$head == "Medicines"] + 475000
# Planted. A salary bill drawn at the treasury, not in the department's books
feb <- treasury_exp$month == as.Date("2025-02-01") & treasury_exp$head == "Salaries"
treasury_exp$amount[feb] <- treasury_exp$amount[feb] + 125000
rm(heads, nov, feb)
```

Both tables have one row per month and head. We join them, compute the difference, and keep the cells that differ.

```{r}
compare <- full_join(dept_exp, treasury_exp, by = join_by(month, head), suffix = c("_dept", "_treasury")) |>
  mutate(difference = amount_treasury - amount_dept)

compare |>
  filter(difference != 0) |>
  select(month, head, amount_dept, amount_treasury, difference)
```

Five cells differ. Their pattern tells the story. Let us total the differences by head for the year.

```{r}
compare |>
  summarise(difference = sum(difference), .by = head)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
by_head <- compare |> summarise(difference = sum(difference), .by = head)
```

The difference in medicines is ₹`r inr(compare$difference[compare$head == "Medicines" & compare$month == as.Date("2024-10-01")])` in October and the same amount the other way in September. Over the year it nets to zero. It is a timing difference. The department booked a bill in September that the treasury passed in October. In November, minor works is ₹`r lakh(310000)` lakh lower at the treasury and office expenses ₹`r lakh(310000)` lakh higher. The total spent is the same, so this is a **misclassification** of one bill. It does not change the total, but it changes what each head shows, and a minor work booked as office expenses may avoid the checks that apply to works. Salaries in February is ₹`r inr(by_head$difference[by_head$head == "Salaries"])` higher at the treasury, with nothing to offset it. A bill was drawn on the department's authority and paid, but the department has no record of it. Like the self cheque, it is the item to pursue first, starting with the bill itself at the treasury.

## A suggested workflow

1. **Ask for the auditee's own reconciliations** and test them first. Note old items and balancing figures.
2. **Get both records independently**, with opening and closing balances, and record a hash of each file. Check that each is complete.
3. **Bring both sides to one shape.** Direction, positive amount, cleaned references, and party names in one form.
4. **Match exact pairs** on reference and amount, with `na_matches = "never"` and `relationship = "one-to-one"`. Use the matched pairs to learn the usual delay.
5. **Match on amount and date** with an inequality join, using a tolerance and window chosen from the data.
6. **Resolve one to one**, by the closest date, then the smallest difference, then the same party, so that no item is used twice.
7. **Search small combinations** of items within a party and a window, for one item that settles several.
8. **Match references typed wrongly** with a string distance, keeping the amount equal.
9. **Classify, age and value what is left.** Timing or permanent, and how old. Test the timing items against the next statement.
10. **Present the statement** and check that it closes. Follow up the permanent and old items, the serious ones first.

::: callout-important
## Remember

- Reconciliation explains every difference between two records of the same money. Cross-verification checks a record against an independent one.
- Timing differences clear by themselves. Permanent differences need an entry or an investigation. Old items in a reconciliation are where problems hide.
- Match in steps, from the surest to the weakest, and remove matches at each step. Never let one item match twice.
- A tolerance and a window are choices. Base them on the data, keep them small, and write them down.
- A match is not proof that a transaction is proper, and a statement that closes is not the end of the work.
- The most serious items are often the smallest in number, such as one debit in the bank that the books do not know about.
:::

## Where next

The joins used here are explained in @sec-joins, the inequality joins in @sec-nonequi and the filtering joins in @sec-joins-filter. @sec-joins-audit uses a rolling join to find the rate in force, which can also find the nearest bank entry to a date. String distances are covered in @sec-strsim, and record linkage across whole files, with several fields at once, in @sec-linkage. Duplicates are treated fully in @sec-dup, and gaps in cheque series in @sec-gaps. Dates are covered in @sec-lubridate, and the checking of GSTINs in @sec-regex-validate. A bank statement received as a PDF can be read with @sec-pdfxl-statement, and the files received recorded with a hash as in @sec-file-hash. Checks on the completeness of a ledger are in @sec-jet-complete.

## Try it yourself {#sec-recon-exercises}

These exercises use the tables and objects of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.

1.  **A narrower window.** Repeat steps 2 and 3 with a window of three days instead of seven, starting from `cb_left` and `bs_left`. How many cash book items are matched now, and how many fewer than before?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_cand <- bs_left |>
      inner_join(cb_left |> mutate(from = cb_date - 3, to = cb_date + 3,
                                   low = cb_amount - 1, high = cb_amount + 1),
                 by = join_by(direction, between(bs_date, from, to), between(bs_amount, low, high))) |>
      mutate(day_gap = abs(as.numeric(bs_date - cb_date)), amt_diff = round(bs_amount - cb_amount, 2),
             same_party = cb_party == bs_party)
    ex_step3 <- one_to_one(ex_cand)
    nrow(ex_step3)
    nrow(step3) - nrow(ex_step3)
    ```
    With three days, `r big(nrow(ex_step3))` items are matched, `r nrow(step3) - nrow(ex_step3)` fewer than with seven. `r if (nrow(step3) == nrow(ex_step3)) "E-payments and receipts clear within three days here, so the narrower window loses nothing." else "Those items would fall to the later steps or be left unmatched, so the window must suit the usual delays."`
    :::

2.  **The cheque series.** The society's cheque books for the year ran from 4101 to 5061. Using `cb`, find cheque numbers in the cash book that are used more than once, and numbers outside the series.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_chq <- cb |> filter(!is.na(cb_chq)) |> mutate(no = as.integer(cb_chq))
    ex_twice <- ex_chq |> filter(n() > 1, .by = no)
    ex_outside <- ex_chq |> filter(no < 4101 | no > 5061)
    ex_twice |> select(cb_id, cb_date, cb_ref, cb_amount)
    ex_outside |> select(cb_id, cb_date, cb_ref, cb_amount)
    ```
    `r nrow(ex_twice)` entries share the number `r ex_twice$cb_chq[1]`, and `r nrow(ex_outside)` numbers lie outside the series. The typing errors found in step 5 explain all of them. Simple checks on the series, as in @sec-gaps, catch such errors before any matching begins.
    :::

3.  **Old items only.** From `left`, list the items older than 60 days with their amounts, and find their total in ₹ lakh.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_old <- left |>
      filter(age_days > 60) |>
      select(side, date, age_days, amount, detail)
    ex_old
    round(sum(ex_old$amount) / 1e5, 2)
    ```
    `r nrow(ex_old)` items are older than 60 days, worth ₹`r round(sum(ex_old$amount) / 1e5, 2)` lakh in all. They are the self cheque and the two stale cheques, the three items that matter most.
    :::

4.  **Unsupported credit by month.** Using `itc`, total the credit on invoices not reported by suppliers for each month of claim. In which month was it highest?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_month <- itc |>
      filter(status == "Not reported by supplier") |>
      summarise(invoices = n(), credit = sum(tax), .by = claimed_in) |>
      arrange(desc(credit))
    ex_month
    ```
    The highest was in `r format(ex_month$claimed_in[1], "%B %Y")`, with ₹`r inr(ex_month$credit[1])` on `r ex_month$invoices[1]` invoices. A month with an unusual amount of unsupported credit is a good place to start asking for documents.
    :::

5.  **Treasury differences by month.** Using `compare`, find the net difference for each month across all heads. Which months differ in total, and which differ only within heads?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_tm <- compare |>
      summarise(net = sum(difference), cells = sum(difference != 0), .by = month) |>
      filter(cells > 0)
    ex_tm
    ```
    `r sum(ex_tm$net != 0)` months differ in total, `r paste(format(ex_tm$month[ex_tm$net != 0], "%B %Y"), collapse = ", ")`. `r paste(format(ex_tm$month[ex_tm$net == 0], "%B %Y"), collapse = ", ")` differs only within heads, with a net of zero, which is the mark of a misclassification.
    :::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `str_extract()`, `str_remove()` | stringr | Takes the cheque or invoice number out of a reference, and removes leading zeros |
| `inner_join()`, `left_join()`, `full_join()` | dplyr | Matches items on a key, and compares totals by month and head |
| `join_by()` with `between()` | dplyr | Matches amounts within a tolerance and dates within a window |
| `na_matches = "never"`, `relationship = "one-to-one"` | dplyr | Stops missing keys matching each other, and stops one item matching twice |
| `cross_join()` | dplyr | Pairs every item with every other, for a small example |
| `anti_join()` | dplyr | Keeps the items not matched at each step |
| `add_count()` | dplyr | Counts the candidates of each item |
| `combn()`, `colSums()` | base R | Lists small combinations of items and their totals |
| `stringdist()`, `amatch()` | stringdist | Finds cheque numbers and GSTINs typed wrongly |
| `cut()` | base R | Puts the age of each item into a band |
| `case_when()` | dplyr | Classifies each item as timing or permanent |
| `coalesce()` | dplyr | Treats missing amounts as zero |
| `filter(n() > 1, .by = )` | dplyr | Finds invoices claimed twice and cheque numbers used twice |
| `str_to_upper()` | stringr | Writes party names in one form on both sides |
| `lag()` | dplyr | Previous balance, to check the running balance of a statement |
| `%%` | base R | Tests whether a difference is divisible by 9 |
| `pivot_wider()` | tidyr | Shows age bands with one column for each side |
| `kable()` | knitr | Prints the reconciliation statement |
